title: Iran Warns Gulf States of Retaliation Against Energy Sites If U.S. Strikes Resume
excerpt: Tehran delivered the threat through diplomatic channels to Saudi Arabia, Qatar, Turkey, and Pakistan after Trump warned of hitting Iran's energy infrastructure, putting Gulf allies in a bind between Washington and Tehran.
body:
• Iran's foreign minister warned Saudi, Qatari, Turkish, and Pakistani counterparts that any new U.S. strikes would trigger retaliation against Gulf energy infrastructure
  • The warning came after Trump threatened on July 28 to target Iran's energy network; Saudi Crown Prince MBS subsequently urged Trump to delay military action
  • Iran's threat list includes refineries, electricity grids, water infrastructure, and oil fields across the Gulf region
  • Trump agreed on August 2 to cancel a planned attack "subject to being able to rapidly make a deal," but a proposed Hormuz deal remains far from settled

Iran has warned Gulf states that any renewed American military strike on its territory will trigger retaliation against critical energy infrastructure across the region, according to a Reuters exclusive citing five sources familiar with the diplomatic exchanges.

The warning was delivered through a burst of high-level contacts after President Donald Trump threatened on July 28 to strike Iran's energy network. Iranian Foreign Minister Abbas Araqchi spoke with his Saudi, Turkish, and Qatari counterparts, as well as Pakistan's army chief, urging them to use their influence with Washington to prevent another round of attacks.

The Threat in Detail

Araqchi's message was consistent across every conversation, according to a senior regional diplomat: "We're ready to retaliate, but finding a diplomatic solution is the best way to avoid wider escalation and destruction across the region."

One Gulf source described the warning as "unequivocal" — if America targeted Iran's infrastructure, Tehran would strike Gulf energy facilities and other regional targets. An Iranian official spelled out a list that includes refineries, electricity grids, water infrastructure, transport networks, and oil fields.

"They still remember Saudi Arabia's Aramco."

— Senior Iranian official, referring to the 2019 drone strikes on Abqaiq and Khurais

The reference to the September 2019 attacks on Saudi Aramco facilities, which temporarily knocked out more than half the kingdom's crude output, was a pointed reminder of Gulf vulnerability.

Diplomatic Fallout

Saudi Crown Prince Mohammed bin Salman spoke with Trump after receiving Iran's warning, urging him to delay military action and return to negotiations. Qatar, Oman, and Saudi Arabia have all pressed Washington to resume talks with Tehran.

"Saudi Arabia believes further escalation will only bring more destruction," one Gulf source told Reuters. "That is why it urged Trump to give diplomacy a chance."

Trump agreed on August 2 to cancel a planned attack "subject to being able to rapidly make a deal." But the path to a settlement remains fraught. A proposed arrangement brokered by Oman would give Iran control over ships entering the Gulf through the Strait of Hormuz — a concession U.S. officials have repeatedly said they would never accept.

India and Diaspora Impact

The escalation directly threatens the 9 million Indian nationals living and working across the Gulf, particularly in the UAE, Saudi Arabia, Qatar, and Kuwait. India imports roughly 60% of its crude oil from Gulf producers, and any strike on energy infrastructure would send shockwaves through global oil markets and Indian fuel prices.

The Strait of Hormuz, which carried roughly a fifth of the world's oil and gas shipments before the war, has been largely closed by Iran since hostilities began. Bunker fuel sales at the UAE's Fujairah port have more than halved in the first half of 2026.

What's Next

From Tehran's perspective, Trump now faces two unpalatable choices: escalate a conflict that could engulf the Gulf and disrupt global energy supplies, or accept a negotiated outcome that falls short of the decisive victory Washington seeks. The principal obstacle, according to the senior regional diplomat, is Washington's reluctance to let Tehran emerge claiming victory.

"The United States wants something it can present as proof that it won the war," the diplomat said. In the meantime, Gulf states remain caught between an ally demanding loyalty and a neighbor threatening destruction.
